description: We’re a six member team interested in space exploration, software development, AI, and data visualization. We’re building a Martian Map that combines NASA data, interactive 3D terrain, and an AI mission assistant to help explorers plan excursions and understand their return options when conditions change. Our team is complete; we are not recruiting additional members.
summary:
MARS RETURN is a mission rehearsal tool for a Marswalk in Jezero Crater. It plans round trips from a hypothetical base to five real Perseverance sampling sites over real MRO CTX terrain, and answers the question every walk must answer: can we still get back?

Most planners stop at "the route fits the time budget." MARS RETURN also asks whether base can still see you. It computes line of sight from the base over the real terrain and reports the longest time out of contact. On the default route to Sid, the walk fits with over an hour to spare, yet the crew is out of sight of base for about an hour at a stretch.

Rehearse the walk, pause anywhere, change the scenario, and make the call yourself before the planner answers: return now, or continue? An assistant then explains the result without ever calculating: every number it says is traced to the saved plan.
details:
Live demo: https://mars-return.onrender.com

Source code: https://github.com/Fadhil006/mars-return

WHAT IT DOES

MARS RETURN is a mission rehearsal tool for a Marswalk in Jezero Crater. Choose one of five real Perseverance sampling sites (Sid, Roubion, Rochette, Brac, Issole). The planner finds two routes from a hypothetical base over real MRO CTX elevation at 20 m: the shortest, and one that avoids slope. For each it gives the round-trip time, time on site, reserve and the margin left in the time budget, in a 2D map and in 3D terrain.

Then it asks the question other planners skip: can base still see you? It computes line of sight from a hypothetical base mast to every cell of the terrain, shades the ground the base cannot see, and reports the total and longest continuous time out of contact, including time spent at a site the base cannot see. The base sees only about a quarter of the area. Every route fits the time budget, but three of the five sites break a 15-minute contact rule. On the default route to Sid, the walk fits with 1 h 16 min to spare, yet the crew is out of sight of base for 1 h 03 min at a stretch.

HOW IT WORKS

- Rehearsal: play the walk, pause anywhere, add a hypothetical event (a blocked corridor, less time left) and request return options.

- Decide first: the planner's options stay hidden until you make the call, "Return now" or "Continue, then return", against a 10-second countdown. Then the app shows both options and says how your call compares with the planner's result. Committing before seeing a model's answer reduces over-reliance on it (Buçinca et al., CSCW 2021).

- Return envelope: every point from which the crew can still walk home in time.

- Stress test: closes the way home at points along the route, one at a time, and checks whether a detour still fits.

- Evidence: a source card for every site, with NASA's sample inventory and the limits of each location record.

- Radiation: a per-excursion dose estimate from the surface dose Curiosity's RAD instrument measured (labelled as Gale Crater data, not Jezero).

- Mission report: one page with every result and its sources.

HOW AI IS USED

The assistant explains results but never calculates. It reads the saved plan through a trusted lookup, and every number in an answer is shown next to the stored value it repeats ("11 of 11 numbers traced to planner output"). Safety, hazard and radiation questions get fixed answers that state what the planner does not model. With an Anthropic key, a Claude model can word the answers; any answer whose numbers or citations do not match the plan is discarded. The public demo runs on fixed templates, with no model.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

On Earth, climbers and pilots get into trouble by pressing on when the numbers say turn back. On Mars, the walk home is the plan that matters, and losing contact with base matters as much as running out of time. MARS RETURN makes both visible on real terrain before anyone walks, and lets crews and planners practise the turnaround call itself, not just read a number. The same approach would work for any site with an elevation model and a base position, on Mars or the Moon.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

- Contact with base as a second verdict next to the time margin, computed from real terrain (Artemis EVA planning limits time without line of sight to the lander).

- A planner that tests the person: you decide before it answers.

- An AI assistant that has to show where every number came from, instead of asking to be trusted.

VALIDATION

- 134 backend and 42 frontend automated tests.

- Route search checked against an independent Dijkstra implementation.

- The line-of-sight code tested on synthetic terrain with known answers.

- 125 Perseverance rover positions compared with the orbital elevation: mean difference −0.82 m, standard deviation 1.98 m.

- Per-site contact results recorded in docs/validation.md.

TOOLS

Python, FastAPI, NumPy, rasterio; TypeScript, React, Vite, Three.js; Docker on Render. Built with the help of Claude Code.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Honesty about what is real and what is assumed. The terrain, imagery, sampling sites and rover positions are real NASA data. The base, mast height, walking speed, time budget, contact rule and blocked corridor are hypothetical inputs, labelled on screen. Line of sight is geometric only: no antennas, relays or radio effects. The 20 m terrain cannot show boulders or ripples, and constant speed ignores fatigue. Missing data is shown, never filled in. Nothing here is certified navigation, communications or safety guidance.
